name: Testing Effect
description: People remember information better when they have to actively retrieve it than when they only re-read it. In interface terms, doing and recalling usually teaches better than passively seeing the same thing again.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to onboarding, help flows, product education, and learning products: guided tasks, short knowledge checks, and 'try it yourself' interactions often create stronger retention than passive walkthroughs.
prevalence_note: Common in learning-experience design, edtech, and increasingly in SaaS onboarding/product-education practice; not as universal in baseline UI design as Gestalt or Fitts's Law, but far from obscure.

findings.description: Meta-analytic review across the testing-vs-restudy literature confirms the testing effect as a reliable phenomenon and identifies test format as a key moderator: initial recall tests (free/cued recall) produce larger testing benefits than recognition-format tests. Existing semantic-elaboration accounts receive only limited support, favoring effortful-processing and retrieval-based theoretical accounts instead.
findings.source_title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect.

findings.description: Repeated retrieval practice (taking recall tests without feedback) produced substantially greater retention than repeated restudy on delayed final tests (2 days or 1 week later), reversing the pattern seen on an immediate (5-minute) test where restudy still had the edge; students' confidence in their own retention did not track this benefit — restudying increased confidence more than testing did, despite testing producing better actual retention.

applications.title: A teacher's 'blank page' method turns any classroom moment into retrieval practice
applications.description: Instructional coach Molly Ostergaard describes a classroom technique she calls the 'blank page approach': instead of rereading notes or waiting for a study guide, students are asked to reconstruct what they know from memory onto a blank sheet -- as a brain dump, concept map, flash card, or sketchnote -- at any point during a unit, not just before a formal assessment. She frames the technique explicitly around retrieval practice and the testing effect, crediting cognitive scientist Pooja Agarwal's research reframing learning as 'getting information out of students' heads' rather than just into them.
applications.ethical_note: A retrieval-practice technique applied directly for students' own learning benefit, with no persuasive or commercial intent.
